passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: There is a seductive simplicity in the idea that an action is right if it produces the most good and wrong if it does not. On this accounting the moral life becomes a kind of arithmetic: tally the pleasure and the suffering that an act sets loose in the world, subtract the second from the first, and let the remainder decide. Much of the appeal lies in its refusal of favoritism, for the calculation counts each person's welfare as one and none as more than one. Yet the same impartiality that makes the view attractive is what unsettles us when we follow it to its edges. If only the sum of outcomes matters, then a lie, a betrayal, even the sacrifice of an innocent, could be not merely excused but required, provided the ledger came out ahead. The arithmetic promises to free us from prejudice, and threatens, in the same motion, to free us from every restraint we thought morality existed to impose.

Against this stands an older intuition, that certain things are owed regardless of what they yield. To treat a person as a mere means to someone else's benefit, on this view, is to violate something in them that no favorable total can repay, because their worth is not a quantity to be weighed but a status to be honored. The strength of the position is that it names what the arithmetic leaves out, the sense that we are answerable to persons and not only to sums. Its weakness is the mirror image of that strength, for a duty held absolutely can bind us to disaster, forbidding the lie that would turn away a murderer at the door. Perhaps neither picture is meant to be inhabited alone. What each exposes is the poverty of the other, and the honest moralist may be the one who refuses to silence either voice, enduring the tension rather than resolving it too cheaply.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Philosophy, Ch. 9 (Normative Moral Theory)

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that
choices: moral rightness is best settled by calculating which action produces the most overall good
both the outcome-based and the duty-based views capture something the other omits, and the tension between them may be irreducible
certain actions are forbidden absolutely, whatever consequences follow from refusing them
morality is ultimately a matter of personal preference rather than reasoned principle
questions.explain: The author says 'neither picture is meant to be inhabited alone' and praises the moralist who refuses 'to silence either voice.'

questions.stem: The reference to the lie that would 'turn away a murderer at the door' serves primarily to
choices: show that lying is always morally permissible
illustrate how an absolute duty can lead to disastrous results
prove that consequences are the only thing that matters
demonstrate that most people are dishonest under pressure
questions.explain: The example is offered to show a 'duty held absolutely can bind us to disaster,' the weakness that mirrors the view's strength.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the view that morality is 'a kind of arithmetic' is best described as
choices: wholly persuaded by its impartiality
contemptuous of anyone who holds it
appreciative of its appeal yet wary of where it leads
indifferent to its merits and flaws
questions.explain: The author grants the view's 'seductive simplicity' and impartial appeal while warning that it 'threatens ... to free us from every restraint.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'status' most nearly means
choices: a person's rank in society
a temporary legal classification
a standing or worth that does not vary with circumstance
a passing condition or mood
questions.explain: The 'status to be honored' is contrasted with 'a quantity to be weighed,' meaning an inherent worth rather than a social rank.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author regards a purely duty-based ethics as
choices: flawless in its treatment of moral conflicts
valuable for naming what the arithmetic omits, yet dangerous when held without exception
identical in practice to the outcome-based view
concerned only with the consequences of actions
questions.explain: The duty view's 'strength is that it names what the arithmetic leaves out,' but an absolute duty 'can bind us to disaster.'

questions.stem: Which situation best captures the conflict the author leaves unresolved?
choices: a doctor who saves five patients by quietly letting one healthy visitor die for their organs, producing the greater total good at the cost of using a person as a means
a shopper choosing between two brands of equal price and quality
a student deciding how many hours to study for an exam
a citizen voting for the candidate she personally prefers
questions.explain: The transplant case pits the greatest total good against the refusal to treat a person 'as a mere means,' the very tension the author declines to resolve.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: It is tempting to hold that we know something only when we could not possibly be wrong about it, and the temptation has a long and honorable history. If a belief might be mistaken, the reasoning goes, then it is not yet knowledge but merely opinion dressed in confidence, and the philosopher's task is to strip away everything that doubt can touch until only the indubitable remains. The trouble is that almost nothing survives this test. The senses deceive us, memory falters, and even the reasoning we trust to catch these errors is itself a faculty we cannot step outside to check. Pushed to its conclusion, the demand for certainty does not purify our knowledge; it abolishes it, leaving us unable to claim that we know the sun will rise or that the floor will hold. A standard so severe that nothing can meet it tells us less about knowledge than about the standard.

A more modest proposal is that knowing does not require the impossibility of error, only its responsible exclusion. On this view I can know that the floor will hold even while granting that, in some far-fetched sense, it might not, because knowledge is not a fortress immune to every conceivable assault but a claim held on good grounds and open to revision. This is harder to accept than it sounds, for it asks us to live with a permanent gap between being justified and being guaranteed. Yet the alternative, waiting for a certainty that never comes, is not caution but paralysis. The fallibilist does not abandon the pursuit of truth; he abandons only the fantasy that truth must announce itself with a seal no doubt can break. To know, on this account, is to have earned a belief, not to have escaped forever the possibility of being wrong.

questions.stem: The passage's central argument is that
choices: genuine knowledge requires the complete impossibility of error
we can never know anything at all
knowledge can rest on good grounds without ruling out every conceivable error
the senses are a reliable source of absolute certainty
questions.explain: The author endorses the 'modest proposal' that knowing 'does not require the impossibility of error, only its responsible exclusion.'

questions.stem: The statement that a standard 'so severe that nothing can meet it tells us less about knowledge than about the standard' serves to
choices: reject the demand for certainty by turning its own failure back on itself
prove that the senses never deceive us
defend the view that knowledge is impossible
argue that all standards of knowledge are equally useful
questions.explain: The line uses the standard's own failure, that 'nothing can meet it,' as grounds for doubting the standard rather than knowledge.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the demand for absolute certainty is
choices: reverent, treating it as the only path to truth
critical, regarding it as self-defeating
playful and unserious
entirely neutral and undecided
questions.explain: The author says the demand 'does not purify our knowledge; it abolishes it,' a self-defeating result.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'indubitable' most nearly means
choices: difficult to understand
widely believed by everyone
impossible to doubt
only recently discovered
questions.explain: The philosopher strips away 'everything that doubt can touch until only the indubitable remains,' meaning what cannot be doubted.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author would regard the belief that the sun will rise as
choices: mere opinion with no claim to be knowledge
something we can know despite its bare possibility of being false
certain beyond any conceivable doubt
impossible to hold responsibly
questions.explain: The fallibilist can 'know that the floor will hold even while granting that ... it might not,' and the sun is treated the same way.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most undermine the fallibilist position the author defends?
choices: that people sometimes revise beliefs they once held with confidence
that no belief can count as knowledge unless error in it is strictly impossible
that the senses occasionally mislead us
that some claims are held on better grounds than others
questions.explain: Fallibilism depends on denying that knowledge requires the impossibility of error; if that requirement held, the position would collapse.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: The shift from foraging to farming is usually told as an ascent, the moment our ancestors stopped wandering after their food and learned at last to command it. Fields replaced the hunt, granaries replaced the chase, and on the surplus so gathered rose everything we call civilization: cities, writing, priesthoods, kings. It is a satisfying story, and parts of it are true. But the bones tell a more ambiguous tale. The first farmers were often shorter, sicker, and more worn by labor than the foragers they succeeded, their teeth marked by a narrower diet, their bodies by the new diseases that crowding and cattle brought. A people who had once drawn on the whole variety of a landscape now staked their survival on a few domesticated grains, and when those grains failed, there was no wilderness left to fall back upon.

Why, then, did farming spread, if it cost so much? Part of the answer is that its costs were invisible to those who paid them, accruing slowly across generations that had no memory of another way to live. Part is that farming, for all its burdens, could feed more mouths from the same ground, and a crowded village, however unhealthy, could outlast and overrun a thinner band of hunters. What triumphed, in other words, was not the happier life but the more numerous one, and the two are easily confused. To read the rise of agriculture as simple progress is to assume that whatever wins must have been better, when the record suggests only that it was better at multiplying. The lesson is less comforting than the usual story, and harder to unlearn: a way of life can conquer the world without ever having made its people well.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax World History Volume 1: to 1500 (the Neolithic Revolution and early agricultural societies)

questions.stem: The central point of the passage is that
choices: the shift to agriculture was an unambiguous improvement in human life
farming spread because it made human life healthier and easier
agriculture prevailed by supporting larger populations, not by making people better off
foraging societies were incapable of producing any surplus
questions.explain: The author concludes that 'what triumphed ... was not the happier life but the more numerous one,' distinguishing success from improvement.

questions.stem: The description of the first farmers as 'shorter, sicker, and more worn by labor' functions primarily to
choices: complicate the familiar story of agriculture as pure progress
prove that foragers never suffered from any disease
argue that farming produced no surplus at all
show that modern diets are healthier than ancient ones
questions.explain: The bodily evidence is offered as 'a more ambiguous tale' against the story of farming as an unqualified 'ascent.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the familiar story of farming as an 'ascent' is
choices: wholly accepting of it
skeptical, granting its partial truth while resisting its conclusion
outraged at those who tell it
wholly indifferent to it
questions.explain: The author calls the story 'satisfying' and admits 'parts of it are true,' yet insists 'the bones tell a more ambiguous tale.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'accruing' most nearly means
choices: disappearing over time
accumulating gradually
being paid off in full
becoming visible all at once
questions.explain: The costs were 'invisible' because they were 'accruing slowly across generations,' meaning building up little by little.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author considers the spread of farming to be evidence that
choices: the way of life that prevails is not necessarily the one that serves people best
human beings always choose whatever improves their health
population size has no effect on which societies endure
foraging was doomed by its own inefficiency
questions.explain: The author warns against assuming 'that whatever wins must have been better,' since farming was merely 'better at multiplying.'

questions.stem: Which modern situation is most analogous to the pattern the author identifies?
choices: a technology that spreads widely because it lets more people be supported, even though it lowers the quality of their daily lives
a craft that dies out because no one is willing to practice it
a diet adopted because rigorous studies prove it extends lifespan
a custom preserved purely for its beauty despite serving no function
questions.explain: The pattern is a way of life prevailing by 'multiplying' rather than by improving lives, which the spreading technology mirrors.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: When two worlds that had developed in isolation were joined after 1492, the traffic between them was not only in ships and soldiers but in seeds, animals, and unseen microbes, and it is this quieter cargo that reshaped the planet most profoundly. Maize and the potato crossed one way and would eventually feed populations from Ireland to China; horses, wheat, and sugarcane crossed the other and remade the diets and landscapes of two continents. To narrate the encounter only as a story of conquest and gold is to miss the deeper rearrangement, in which the very biology of the world was shuffled and dealt out again. Whole cuisines we now think of as ancient and national, the tomato in Italy, the chili in India, are the recent offspring of this collision, so thoroughly naturalized that their foreign birth has been forgotten.

Yet the same exchange that enriched the world's tables also emptied its villages. The microbes that traveled with the newcomers found populations with no inherited defense against them, and across the Americas disease did what no army could have, killing on a scale that beggars the vocabulary of war. To celebrate the new abundance without reckoning this loss would be a kind of accounting fraud, crediting the ledger while hiding the debit. What the period demands of us is a double vision, the capacity to see that the same event was, at once, one of the great enrichments and one of the great catastrophes of human history, and that these are not two stories to be told in turn but one story that refuses to resolve into either. The exchange gave and it took, and it did not consult the people whose worlds it remade.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax World History Volume 2: from 1400 (the Columbian Exchange and early modern global connections)

questions.stem: The passage is chiefly concerned with arguing that
choices: the joining of the two worlds was primarily a story of conquest and gold
the exchange after 1492 was at once a great enrichment and a great catastrophe that cannot be separated
the movement of crops mattered far more than the movement of people
the new diseases were a minor footnote to an era of abundance
questions.explain: The author calls for 'a double vision' seeing 'one of the great enrichments and one of the great catastrophes' as 'one story that refuses to resolve into either.'

choices: show how thoroughly the exchange reshaped even cuisines now thought ancient and native

suggest that these foods were always present in those places
questions.explain: These dishes are 'the recent offspring of this collision, so thoroughly naturalized that their foreign birth has been forgotten.'

questions.stem: The author regards celebrating the new abundance without acknowledging the loss as
choices: a reasonable emphasis on the exchange's benefits
a form of dishonest accounting
the only responsible way to tell the story
a harmless simplification
questions.explain: To celebrate abundance without the loss 'would be a kind of accounting fraud, crediting the ledger while hiding the debit.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'naturalized' most nearly means
choices: returned to a wild state
granted legal citizenship
so absorbed into a place that it seems native
studied by natural scientists
questions.explain: The foods are 'so thoroughly naturalized that their foreign birth has been forgotten,' meaning they now seem native.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author considers the 'quieter cargo' of seeds and microbes to have been
choices: less important than the movement of soldiers and gold
more transformative of the world than the conquest itself
beneficial in every one of its effects
unrelated to the demographic collapse in the Americas
questions.explain: The author says 'it is this quieter cargo that reshaped the planet most profoundly,' beyond the story 'of conquest and gold.'

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most support the author's call for a 'double vision' of the exchange?
choices: a region whose population was devastated by imported disease in the same decades that its farmland grew far more productive from imported crops
a region that received new crops but was never touched by any new disease
a war whose casualties were caused entirely by soldiers rather than illness
a cuisine that developed in complete isolation from foreign ingredients
questions.explain: A single region enriched and devastated at once embodies the claim that gain and loss were 'one story that refuses to resolve into either.'

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: For a brief span after the war, the country attempted something it had never seriously tried before: to remake a society founded on bondage into one founded on equal citizenship, and to do so by law, in a single generation. Amendments were written into the Constitution that abolished slavery, promised equal protection, and forbade the denial of the vote on account of race. Men who had been counted as property a decade earlier now sat in legislatures and sent representatives to the capital. Read forward from its beginning, the period can look like the opening of a door long held shut. But history is not read forward by those who live it, and the same door, we know, would be forced closed again within a dozen years, its promises left standing on the page while the world beneath them was quietly rearranged to defeat them.

What defeated Reconstruction was not the repeal of its guarantees, for they were never repealed; it was the discovery that a right written down is not yet a right secured. A vote that cannot be safely cast is a vote in name only, and an equality announced by the state but unenforced by it becomes a kind of official fiction, more useful to the comfortable than to those it was meant to protect. The lesson later generations drew from the period was accordingly double-edged. It showed how much could be achieved by law, and how little, when law is severed from the power and the will to make it real. To honor Reconstruction as a triumph or dismiss it as a failure is equally to miss its instruction, which is that the two can inhabit the same events, and that a promise and its betrayal are sometimes written in the same hand.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that Reconstruction
choices: succeeded completely in remaking Southern society
collapsed because its constitutional amendments were formally repealed
showed both how much law can achieve and how little it achieves when unenforced
proved that written guarantees are always sufficient to secure rights
questions.explain: The period 'showed how much could be achieved by law, and how little, when law is severed from the power and the will to make it real.'

questions.stem: The image of a 'door long held shut' that 'would be forced closed again' primarily serves to
choices: capture both the opening of new possibilities and their subsequent defeat
argue that no progress of any kind was made during the period
suggest that the amendments were never actually written
prove that doors are a common feature of legislatures
questions.explain: The door 'long held shut' that is then 'forced closed again' figures both the promise and its reversal.

questions.stem: The author regards the labels 'triumph' and 'failure' as applied to Reconstruction as
choices: equally mistaken because both miss the period's real lesson
accurate depending only on one's political views
useful shorthand that captures the period well
irrelevant to any serious study of history
questions.explain: To 'honor Reconstruction as a triumph or dismiss it as a failure is equally to miss its instruction.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'severed' most nearly means
choices: cut off or separated
sharply criticized
formally approved
briefly interrupted
questions.explain: Law 'severed from the power and the will to make it real' means law cut off from enforcement.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that a legal right is genuinely secured only when
choices: it has been written into a constitution
it is backed by the power and will to enforce it
it is popular with the comfortable majority
it has never been challenged in a court
questions.explain: 'A right written down is not yet a right secured'; what was missing was 'the power and the will to make it real.'

questions.stem: Which contemporary situation best illustrates the lesson the author draws from Reconstruction?
choices: a law guaranteeing a benefit that goes unclaimed because the state provides no means to enforce it
a law that is formally repealed by a later legislature
a right that is both written down and vigorously protected in practice
a custom that persists even though no law requires it
questions.explain: The lesson is that 'a right written down is not yet a right secured'; an unenforced guarantee is a right 'in name only.'

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: Before the factory and the canal, most people worked to a rhythm set by the sun and the season, and the line between labor and life was blurred by a hundred small liberties: the errand run midmorning, the task set down when a neighbor called, the long idleness of winter. The transformations of the early nineteenth century did not merely move this work from farm to workshop; they rebuilt its very measure. Where a task had once been finished when it was done, it was now timed, and the clock on the wall became a quiet sovereign, dividing the day into units that could be bought. To sell one's labor by the hour is to accept that the hour belongs, for its duration, to another, and this was a stranger bargain than it now appears to a people who had rarely thought of their time as a thing that could be owned at all.

It would be sentimental to mourn the older way without remembering its poverty, for the same market that disciplined the worker also filled the shops with goods that no previous generation could have dreamed of owning, and offered, to some, an escape from the narrow fate of birth. The honest reckoning is not a lament but a balance. Something was gained in abundance and mobility, and something was lost in autonomy and rhythm, and the gain and the loss fell, as they usually do, on different people and in different measure. What makes the period worth studying is precisely that it will not sit still as either a rise or a fall. It was the hinge on which a whole way of living turned, and those who lived through it felt, often at once, the promise of the new order and the quiet expropriation of a freedom they had not known they possessed until it was gone.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax U.S. History (the market revolution and the transformation of Northern labor)

questions.stem: The passage principally argues that the changes it describes
choices: improved daily life in every important respect
simply relocated existing work without altering its nature
brought both new abundance and a loss of autonomy that fell unevenly on different people
were mourned by everyone who lived through them
questions.explain: The author calls for 'a balance': 'something was gained in abundance and mobility, and something was lost in autonomy and rhythm.'

questions.stem: The description of the clock as 'a quiet sovereign' primarily serves to
choices: convey how thoroughly measured time came to govern the working day
praise the punctuality of nineteenth-century workers

suggest that workers came to admire their employers
questions.explain: The clock 'divid[es] the day into units that could be bought,' ruling the day as a 'sovereign' would.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward mourning the older rhythm of work is
choices: wholehearted, treating the change as pure loss
guarded, warning that such mourning forgets the older way's poverty
dismissive of the idea that anything was lost
indifferent to the question entirely
questions.explain: The author calls it 'sentimental to mourn the older way without remembering its poverty' and insists on 'a balance.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'expropriation' most nearly means
choices: a fair exchange of goods
a taking away of something once possessed
a sudden increase in wealth
a public celebration
questions.explain: The 'expropriation of a freedom' names a freedom that was lost, taken from those who 'had not known they possessed' it.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that, before the changes described, most people generally
choices: thought of their time as something that could be bought and sold
did not conceive of their time as a possession that could be owned
worked longer and more tightly regulated hours than afterward
enjoyed a greater abundance of manufactured goods than afterward
questions.explain: The bargain seemed strange 'to a people who had rarely thought of their time as a thing that could be owned at all.'

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's characterization of the change in work?
choices: evidence that farm labor before the period was already governed by strict, externally imposed schedules just as rigid as the factory's
evidence that factories filled shops with new kinds of goods
evidence that some workers escaped the fate of their birth
evidence that winters were often idle on many farms
questions.explain: The author's contrast depends on older work being loosely timed; if it was already rigidly scheduled, the claimed transformation dissolves.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: There is a reflex, older than any argument, by which we take the customs of our own people as the plain shape of the human and treat every departure from them as a deviation to be explained. The food others eat is strange, their manners are wrong, their gods are false, and the measure by which all this is judged is simply the way things are done at home, mistaken for the way things are. Sociologists have a name for this reflex and for the discipline meant to correct it. To see one's own culture as the natural center of the world is ethnocentrism; to suspend that judgment and try to understand a practice within the web of meaning that gives it sense is the harder work of cultural relativism. The first comes to us for free. The second must be learned, and is never learned completely.

Yet relativism, pressed too far, dissolves into a paralysis of its own. If every practice can be judged only from inside its own culture, then no practice can ever be criticized from without, and the cruelties that some societies have visited on the weak acquire an immunity merely by being customary. The observer who set out to cure arrogance arrives, by an unwanted road, at an inability to object to anything at all. The way through is not to abandon understanding but to distinguish it from endorsement. To grasp why a practice makes sense to those who follow it is one act; to decide whether it should continue is another, and the first does not settle the second. Relativism at its best is a method of seeing, not a verdict of approval, and the confusion of the two has done as much harm to the idea as any of its enemies.

questions.stem: The passage's central argument is that cultural relativism
choices: requires approving of every practice one studies
is a method for understanding practices, not a verdict approving them
is simply another name for ethnocentrism
should be abandoned in favor of judging all cultures by one's own
questions.explain: The author holds that 'relativism at its best is a method of seeing, not a verdict of approval.'

questions.stem: The observation that some cruelties can 'acquire an immunity merely by being customary' serves to
choices: show the danger of pressing relativism too far
prove that all cultures are equally cruel
defend ethnocentrism as the safer attitude
argue that customs can never be criticized on any grounds
questions.explain: The line exposes how relativism 'pressed too far' leaves one with 'an inability to object to anything at all.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the ethnocentric reflex is
choices: approving, since it places one's own culture at the natural center
critical, treating it as an error that discipline must correct
neutral and merely descriptive
admiring of its honesty
questions.explain: Ethnocentrism is the 'reflex' that relativism, 'the harder work,' is 'meant to correct.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'reflex' most nearly means
choices: a careful and deliberate decision
an automatic, unexamined response
a reflected mirror image
a physical injury
questions.explain: The 'reflex' is a response that 'comes to us for free,' unlike the relativism that 'must be learned.'

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author sees understanding a practice and endorsing it as
choices: two distinct acts, the first of which does not determine the second
one and the same act
equally impossible to achieve
steps that must always occur in reverse order
questions.explain: 'To grasp why a practice makes sense ... is one act; to decide whether it should continue is another, and the first does not settle the second.'

questions.stem: Which response to an unfamiliar custom best reflects relativism as the author defines it?
choices: studying the custom to understand its meaning to insiders, while reserving judgment about whether it is right
condemning the custom immediately because it differs from one's own
praising the custom simply because it belongs to another culture
refusing to learn anything about the custom at all
questions.explain: Relativism as 'a method of seeing' means understanding a practice from inside while keeping that 'distinct' from approval.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: We like to believe that the self is the one thing we bring into the world already ours, a core of pure individuality that society then either nurtures or represses. The study of socialization suggests something less flattering and more interesting: that the self is not the raw material of social life but one of its products. The child does not arrive with a finished identity awaiting expression; she assembles one, gradually, out of the responses of others, learning who she is by watching who they take her to be. We come to see ourselves, in a sense, reflected in the faces around us, and the image we call our personality is in part a portrait painted by other hands. To say this is not to deny that we are individuals. It is to notice that individuality itself is something we are taught.

This has a consequence we are reluctant to accept, which is that the line between the self and society, so firm in our everyday speech, does not survive close inspection. The values we call our own were once instructions we absorbed before we could weigh them; the desires we experience as most intimately ours were shaped by a world that was choosing them for us long before we imagined we were choosing. None of this makes freedom an illusion, but it does relocate it. Freedom is not the possession of a self that stands outside society, for there is no such self to possess it. It is, more modestly, the capacity to examine what we have been made into and to revise it, a work that uses the very tools society gave us. We are its creatures, and our only route to self-authorship runs through, not around, that fact.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that
choices: the self exists fully formed before any social influence
the self is largely a product of socialization rather than a pre-social core
society has no real influence on individual identity
human freedom is entirely an illusion
questions.explain: The author holds 'the self is not the raw material of social life but one of its products,' assembled 'out of the responses of others.'

questions.stem: The image of 'a portrait painted by other hands' primarily serves to
choices: convey that our sense of self is shaped by how others regard us
argue that people cannot recognize their own faces
prove that painting is more truthful than other arts
suggest that personality is entirely inherited at birth
questions.explain: We 'see ourselves ... reflected in the faces around us,' so identity is 'in part a portrait painted by other hands.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the belief in a self that exists before society is
choices: accepting, treating it as obviously correct
skeptical, regarding it as flattering but unsupported by close inspection
hostile toward anyone who questions it
wholly indifferent
questions.explain: The belief is 'flattering,' but the author says the self and society line 'does not survive close inspection.'

questions.stem: As used in the passage, 'creatures' most nearly means
choices: wild animals
beings shaped and produced by something else
imaginary monsters
wholly independent inventors
questions.explain: To be society's 'creatures' is to be its products, beings it 'made,' consistent with the self as something assembled by others.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author locates human freedom in
choices: a self that stands entirely outside society
the capacity to examine and revise what socialization has made of us
the complete rejection of every value one was taught
the impossibility of ever changing one's identity
questions.explain: Freedom is 'the capacity to examine what we have been made into and to revise it,' using 'the very tools society gave us.'

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most challenge the author's account of the self?
choices: evidence that core features of a person's identity are fixed at birth and remain unchanged regardless of how others treat them
evidence that children imitate the adults around them
evidence that people absorb values before they can evaluate them
evidence that individuals can later reflect on their upbringing
questions.explain: The author claims the self is shaped by others' responses; an identity fixed at birth and immune to them would undermine that claim.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: To the untrained eye, kinship looks like biology wearing a few local costumes. Everywhere there are mothers and fathers, everywhere children, and the anthropologist who catalogues the world's family systems can seem to be merely recording the same natural facts in a hundred dialects. But the closer one looks, the more the biology recedes and the costume turns out to be the substance. In many societies the man a child calls father is not the one who begot him but his mother's brother, or a line of ancestors, or whoever occupies a certain social role; the word we translate as mother may extend to a whole class of women. What counts as a relative, and what that relation demands, is decided not by blood but by rules that vary from people to people, rules that blood by itself could never dictate.

This is why the anthropologist resists the easy assumption that our own arrangement, the small household bound by shared genes, is the natural form from which others deviate. It is one form among many, no more written into nature than the rest, and it answers needs that other systems answer differently. Kinship, properly understood, is less a map of who is related to whom than a scheme for assigning duties, inheritance, loyalty, and care, a way of organizing the cooperation without which no human group survives. Blood may furnish the raw metaphor, but it is the culture that decides what the metaphor will mean, drawing the circle of obligation now wide, now narrow, and filling it with persons that no genealogist would recognize as kin. To study kinship is thus to study not nature's dictates but one of the oldest and most inventive of human institutions.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Anthropology (kinship and descent)

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: In the marketplace a transaction is designed to end. I pay, you deliver, and the moment the exchange is balanced our obligation to each other is discharged; we may walk away as strangers, owing nothing. The gift works by the opposite principle. To give is not to settle an account but to open one, to place the receiver under a debt that a return, when it comes, will not so much cancel as continue. Anthropologists who studied the exchange of gifts in many societies noticed that its purpose was rarely the efficient movement of goods, which markets accomplish better, but the weaving of a bond. What travels in the gift is not only the object but a piece of the relationship, and to refuse to give, to receive, or in time to give back is to decline the relationship itself.

It is tempting to read this as a charming inefficiency, a primitive stage that the invention of money and price at last cleared away. But the temptation should be resisted, for the logic of the gift has not vanished; it has only retreated into the regions of life we most care about. We still give at birthdays and weddings, still bristle at the friend who tries to repay a dinner in exact cash, still sense that to reduce certain exchanges to their market value is to insult them. What the anthropology of the gift reveals is not a curiosity of distant peoples but a grammar we ourselves still speak, one in which the deliberate refusal to balance the books is the very thing that turns a transaction into a tie. The market ends relationships on purpose. The gift, on purpose, refuses to let them end.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Anthropology (economic anthropology: exchange and reciprocity)

questions.stem: The central contrast the passage draws is between

questions.explain: A market transaction 'is designed to end,' whereas 'to give ... is to open' an account and weave 'a bond.'

questions.explain: The author writes 'the temptation should be resisted, for the logic of the gift has not vanished.'

questions.explain: 'The deliberate refusal to balance the books is the very thing that turns a transaction into a tie.'

questions.explain: Offense at repaying an intimate favor in cash is exactly the persistence of gift logic the author describes.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: Power, in its rawest form, is only the ability to make others do what they would not otherwise choose, and a state that possessed nothing more than this would be indistinguishable from a well-armed robber. What separates the two is not the amount of force at their disposal but a quality harder to see, which political thinkers call legitimacy: the widespread belief that a power has the right to command and that its commands ought to be obeyed. A government rules far less by the soldiers it can deploy than by the conviction, carried quietly in the minds of the governed, that its rule is proper. When that conviction is present, laws are mostly kept without the need to enforce them; when it drains away, no quantity of police can supply its absence, and a regime that must compel every act of obedience has already begun to fall.

This exposes a paradox at the heart of political order. The state appears to be the strongest thing in society, and in a sense it is; yet its strength rests on something it cannot simply manufacture, a belief in its right to rule that must be granted by the very people it governs. Legitimacy cannot be seized the way a palace can. It is earned, or inherited, or slowly squandered, and a ruler who forgets this, mistaking the machinery of coercion for the source of his authority, saws at the branch that holds him. The most durable power is thus the power least often used, the authority so accepted that it seldom needs to show its hand. What looks like weakness, the dependence of the mighty on the opinion of the governed, turns out to be the hidden condition of every stable rule, and the tyrant's error is to believe he has escaped it.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Political Science (power, authority, and legitimacy)

questions.explain: A government 'rules far less by the soldiers it can deploy than by the conviction ... that its rule is proper.'

questions.explain: The robber has force but lacks 'legitimacy,' the quality that 'separates the two.'

questions.explain: Such a ruler 'saws at the branch that holds him,' mistaking 'the machinery of coercion for the source of his authority.'

questions.explain: Legitimacy is 'earned, or inherited, or slowly squandered,' set against being gained, so squandered means wastefully lost.

questions.explain: Such a regime 'has already begun to fall,' because coercion 'cannot supply' the missing conviction.

questions.explain: Laws 'kept without the need to enforce them' exemplify authority resting on 'the conviction ... that its rule is proper.'

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: No one ever signed the social contract, and this is the first objection every student raises against it. There was no gathering of free individuals in a state of nature who, weary of mutual fear, agreed to trade a portion of their liberty for the protection of a common power. The scene is a fiction, and its authors mostly knew it. But to dismiss the idea on these grounds is to misunderstand what kind of claim it makes. The contract was never offered as a historical event to be dated and verified; it is a device for asking a question that history cannot answer, namely what arrangements free and equal people could accept as binding on themselves. Its truth, if it has one, is not in the past but in the present, in whether the order we actually live under could have been agreed to by those it governs.

Read this way, the contract becomes less a story about how states began than a standard by which they may be judged. A government that could not have won the consent of reasonable people, that rests on the plain subjection of some to the advantage of others, fails a test the metaphor quietly sets, whatever its origins in conquest or inheritance. This is why the fiction has outlived every attempt to refute it on factual grounds. It was doing something other than reporting facts. It was giving political obligation a foundation in agreement rather than in mere force or custom, and thereby handing the governed a question they could put to any power above them: not merely can you compel me, but could I have consented to this? A regime that cannot bear the question has told us something about itself, and the imaginary contract has done its wholly real work.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Political Science (the social contract tradition)

questions.stem: The central argument of the passage is that the social contract

questions.explain: The contract 'becomes less a story about how states began than a standard by which they may be judged.'

questions.explain: The objection 'misunderstand[s] what kind of claim' the contract makes, which the author goes on to clarify.

questions.explain: The author says 'the fiction has outlived every attempt to refute it' because it does 'wholly real work' as a standard.

questions.explain: The defense rests on the contract providing a usable standard of legitimacy; if it yields no clearer verdict, that defense fails.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: The most disenchanting idea in economics is also its most honest: that we cannot have everything, and that every choice is therefore a small act of loss. Because our time, money, and attention are finite while our wants are not, to spend a resource on one thing is necessarily to withhold it from another, and the true cost of anything is not the price on its tag but the best alternative we gave up to obtain it. Economists call this the opportunity cost, and it is easy to say and hard to feel. The hour spent on one task is not merely an hour; it is every other task that hour might have held. Seen clearly, no choice is free, not because someone charges for it, but because the world will not let us do two things with the same resource at the same time.

There is a temptation to find this bleak, as though economics had come to announce that life is a ledger of sacrifices. But the same principle that names the cost also clarifies the value. If choosing one thing means forgoing another, then to choose well is to know what we are willing to give up, and a person who refuses ever to accept a cost is not richer in possibilities but poorer in direction, forever unwilling to trade any option for any outcome. The discipline of opportunity cost is thus not a counsel of gloom but of seriousness. It asks us to price our choices in the only currency that finally matters, the other lives we might have led, and to decide, knowing the exchange rate, which of them we are prepared to let go. To grasp scarcity is not to mourn abundance but to take one's freedom seriously enough to spend it.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e (scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost)

questions.explain: The author reframes opportunity cost as 'a counsel ... of seriousness,' asking us to know 'what we are willing to give up.'

questions.explain: It illustrates opportunity cost: the hour's 'true cost' is 'the best alternative we gave up.'

questions.explain: The author calls the discipline 'not a counsel of gloom but of seriousness,' resisting the bleak reading.

questions.explain: Weighing the job against 'the other lives we might have led' and knowingly letting one go is exactly the 'seriousness' the author urges.

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: The oldest lesson in economics is that a task broken into parts and shared among specialists is done far more abundantly than by each worker laboring alone. One person drawing the wire, another straightening it, a third cutting, a fourth pointing, and a pin factory produces in a day what a single artisan could scarcely make in a year. From this simple observation an enormous prosperity has been argued into being, and the argument is sound: specialization multiplies output, lowers cost, and has lifted more people from want than any decree of charity ever could. The wealth of modern societies is in large part the compounded yield of this one principle, applied and reapplied until the making of almost anything is divided among hands that never meet and often do not know what the others are for.

And yet the same division that enriches the society can diminish the worker within it. The man who spends his life performing a single motion, one operation of the dozens a finished object requires, gains dexterity at that motion and loses, slowly, the fuller competence of the artisan who once saw a thing through from raw stuff to finished form. He grows rich in output and narrow in scope, a specialist who may no longer understand the whole to which he contributes. To notice this is not to wish the division of labor away, for its fruits are too real and too widely shared to renounce. It is to insist that the ledger has a second column, that the productivity we celebrate is purchased in part with a certain fragmentation of the person, and that a society honest about its wealth will count that cost even as it keeps the gains.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e (the division of labor and gains from specialization)

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: Students are taught to think of revision as the stage where a writer fixes mistakes, tidying commas and repairing spelling once the real work of writing is done. This picture is not merely incomplete; it inverts the truth. The corrections we call editing are the least of what revision means, and to stop there is to polish the surface of a house whose walls are in the wrong place. Real revision is not correction but re-vision, a literal seeing again, in which the writer returns to the draft as a stranger might and asks not whether the sentences are clean but whether the thing is doing what it set out to do. Often the answer is no, and the honest reviser must be willing to move a paragraph that took an hour to write, or to cut it, or to discover that the argument he meant to make is not the one that actually arrived on the page.

This is why revision is harder than drafting, and why so many avoid it. To draft is to bring something into being, which is exhilarating; to revise is to judge what one has made, which requires a colder eye turned on one's own warm labor. The attachment we feel to our sentences, especially the clever ones, is precisely the obstacle, for the phrase we are proudest of is often the one doing the least work, kept not because the writing needs it but because we do. The reviser's discipline is to serve the reader rather than the ego, to ask of every passage what it gives to the person who will read it and to remove whatever survives only because its author loves it. Writing, on this understanding, is not a single act of expression but a long argument between the writer and the draft, and it is in that argument, not the first burst of composition, that most of the meaning is made.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Writing Guide with Handbook (the writing process: revising and editing)

passages.label: Passage
paragraphs: We speak of good writing as though it were a property of the words themselves, a quality that a sentence either has or lacks the way a stone has weight. But no sentence is good in the abstract; it is good for someone, in some situation, toward some end. The plain instruction that saves a life in an emergency would be a failure as a poem, and the poem that moves us to tears would be a catastrophe printed on the side of a medicine bottle. What we are really judging when we praise writing is the fit between a text and its occasion, the match between what was said and the reader, purpose, and moment it was meant to serve. Rhetoric gives this cluster a name, the rhetorical situation, and its first lesson is that there is no writing so excellent that it cannot be made wrong by being addressed to the wrong audience at the wrong time.

This unsettles a flattering belief, that the writer is a solitary craftsman answerable only to his art. In truth the reader is a silent collaborator in every sentence, and to write well is to hold that other person constantly in mind, to anticipate what she knows, fears, doubts, and needs, and to shape the words to meet her. This is not a betrayal of honesty for the sake of persuasion; it is the condition of being understood at all. A truth flung at a reader who is not ready to receive it does not become more true for being ignored. The writer who refuses to consider his audience, priding himself on indifference to their responses, has not risen above rhetoric but merely practiced it badly, addressing no one and reaching them. To take the audience seriously is not to flatter them but to grant that communication, unlike private self-expression, is something that must be completed by another.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Writing Guide with Handbook (the rhetorical situation: audience, purpose, and context)
